content_html:
Key Developments

The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, featuring a surprisingly competitive challenge by Democrat Scott Colom against incumbent GOP Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. With approximately 96% of the vote counted, the contest tightened dramatically on Wednesday morning, with only a few dozen votes separating the candidates at one point before Colom pulled ahead by just over 1,100 votes.

Cindy Hyde-Smith, 67, has served in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. Her challenger, 43-year-old district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian Scott Colom, campaigned heavily on the cost of living and health care issues. President Trump previously won Mississippi by 20 points in the 2024 elections, and the state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, making the exceptionally close race a remarkable development in the Magnolia State.

Key Takeaways

  • Razor-Thin Margin: With 96% of votes in, Scott Colom held a narrow lead of just over 1,100 votes over incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
  • Historical Context: Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, and President Trump carried the state by 20 points in 2024.
  • National Implications: The unresolved Mississippi race, alongside an outstanding contest in Alaska, comes as Democrats have already secured enough Senate flips nationwide to take control of the chamber.

Why It Matters

The unexpected competitiveness of the Mississippi Senate race highlights shifting political dynamics in unexpected regions during the 2026 midterms. While national Democrats secured a slew of surprising wins and multiple chamber flips on Tuesday night—including in states won by double digits by President Trump in 2024—a potential victory by Scott Colom would add an extra seat to their newly secured majority. As local officials continue processing the remaining ballots, the outcome in the Magnolia State remains one of the most closely watched unresolved contests of the cycle.
